title: Numbers
description: Integer, floating-point, bigint, decimal and fraction arithmetic. int is 64-bit signed; bigint is exact up to 4000 decimal digits; float is IEEE 754 binary64, always finite, with no negative zero; decimal is exact base 10; fraction is an exact ratio of two 64-bit integers, always in lowest terms. DIV and MOD pin the two places Python and Rust disagree about negative operands; ROUND pins where they disagree about halves; TO_TEXT pins how a float prints.

entries.name: ADD
entries.summary: Add two integers

notes: Integers are 64-bit signed. Overflow is an error, not a wrap and not a promotion to arbitrary precision.

entries.name: SUB
entries.summary: Subtract the second integer from the first

entries.name: MUL
entries.summary: Multiply two integers

entries.name: DIV
entries.summary: Divide two integers, truncating toward zero
entries.description: Integer division. The rounding direction is pinned by contract because the host languages disagree: Python's // floors toward negative infinity, Rust's / truncates toward zero. This address promises truncation, and every backend is held to it.

notes: TRUNCATES TOWARD ZERO: -7 / 2 is -3, not -4.
A Python backend must NOT use // here. This is the clearest example in the registry of a contract overriding a host language's default.

entries.name: MOD
entries.summary: Remainder of integer division, taking the sign of the dividend
entries.description: The companion to DIV: a == DIV(a,b) * b + MOD(a,b) always holds. Python's % takes the sign of the divisor, so a Python backend must not use it directly.

notes: SIGN OF THE DIVIDEND: -7 mod 2 is -1, not 1.
Consistent with DIV (400-0000004) so that a == DIV(a,b)*b + MOD(a,b).

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smaller of two integers

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The larger of two integers

entries.name: SUM
entries.summary: Add up a list of integers

notes: An empty list sums to 0.
Summed left to right.

entries.name: PARSE_INT
entries.summary: Read an integer from text, or a fallback when it is not one

notes: Never fails; unparseable text returns the fallback.
Accepts optional leading '-' or '+' then ASCII digits, with surrounding whitespace trimmed first. Underscores, other digit systems, and other bases are rejected.

entries.name: ABS
entries.summary: The distance of an integer from zero

notes: The absolute value of the smallest 64-bit integer does not fit, so ABS(-9223372036854775808) is an overflow error. Python's abs would quietly return a bigger number; Rust's abs would panic or wrap by build profile.

entries.name: NEGATE
entries.summary: Flip the sign of an integer

notes: NEGATE(-9223372036854775808) is an overflow error, for the same reason as ABS (400-0000010).
NEGATE(0) is 0; there is no negative zero.

entries.name: POW
entries.summary: Raise an integer to a whole-number power

notes: POW(x, 0) is 1 for every x, including POW(0, 0).
A negative exponent is an error, not a fraction: v0 has no floating point.
Overflow is an error whenever the true result does not fit in 64 bits. POW(-2, 63) is -9223372036854775808 and fits; POW(2, 63) does not.
A backend must not raise overflow for a result that fits, and must not build a huge intermediate before noticing one that does not.

entries.name: CLAMP
entries.summary: Hold an integer inside a range, both ends included

notes: Arguments are value, low, high, in that order.
Both ends are included: CLAMP(value, low, high) is low when value < low, high when value > high, and value otherwise.
low greater than high is an invalid_range error. low equal to high is allowed and always returns that number. Rust's clamp would panic here; Python has no clamp.

entries.name: SIGN
entries.summary: Whether an integer is negative, zero, or positive

notes: Returns exactly -1, 0, or 1. Never fails.

entries.name: ADD_FLOAT
entries.summary: Add two floats

notes: float is IEEE 754 binary64. The result is the exact sum rounded to nearest, ties to even, which every backend gets from its hardware.
FINITE ONLY: a result too large to be finite is an overflow error. NaN and infinity never exist as values.
NO NEGATIVE ZERO: a result of -0.0 is 0.0.

entries.name: SUB_FLOAT
entries.summary: Subtract the second float from the first

notes: Rounded to nearest, ties to even. A result too large to be finite is an overflow error.
NO NEGATIVE ZERO: 0.0 - 0.0 is 0.0, and so is any other difference that would be -0.0.

entries.name: MUL_FLOAT
entries.summary: Multiply two floats

notes: Rounded to nearest, ties to even. A result too large to be finite is an overflow error; a result too small to represent is 0.0.
NO NEGATIVE ZERO: -2.0 * 0.0 is 0.0.

entries.name: DIV_FLOAT
entries.summary: Divide one float by another
entries.description: True division. Unlike DIV (400-0000004) nothing is truncated; the quotient is rounded to the nearest float.

notes: Rounded to nearest, ties to even.
DIVIDING BY ZERO IS AN ERROR, including 0.0 / 0.0. IEEE 754 would give infinity or NaN; this contract never produces either.
A quotient too large to be finite is an overflow error. One too small to represent is 0.0, never -0.0.

entries.name: TO_FLOAT
entries.summary: Convert an integer to a float

notes: Exact for every integer whose magnitude is at most 2^53. Larger integers round to the nearest float, ties to even: 9007199254740993 becomes 9007199254740992.0.

entries.name: TO_INT
entries.summary: Convert a float to an integer, truncating toward zero
entries.description: Drops the fractional part, the same direction DIV (400-0000004) rounds. Use ROUND (400-0000021) first for nearest.

notes: TRUNCATES TOWARD ZERO: 2.9 is 2 and -2.9 is -2.
A value whose truncation does not fit a 64-bit signed integer is an overflow error. It never saturates, which is what Rust's `as i64` would do.

entries.name: ROUND
entries.summary: Round a float to the nearest whole number, halves away from zero
entries.description: The rounding direction is pinned by contract because the host languages disagree: Python's round() sends halves to the nearest even number, Rust's f64::round sends them away from zero. This address promises away from zero.

notes: HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO: 2.5 is 3.0 and -2.5 is -3.0. A Python backend must NOT use round(), which would give 2.
Decided on the exact binary value, never on its printed digits: 0.49999999999999994 is 0.0, because it is below one half.
The result is a float. Use TO_INT (400-0000020) to get an int. NO NEGATIVE ZERO: -0.4 rounds to 0.0.

entries.name: PARSE_FLOAT
entries.summary: Read a float from text, or a fallback when it is not one

notes: Never fails; unparseable text returns the fallback.

Accepts, after trimming surrounding whitespace: an optional '+' or '-', one or more ASCII digits, optionally '.' and one or more digits, optionally 'e' or 'E', an optional sign, and one or more digits. So '3', '-0.5' and '1.5e3' parse; '.5', '5.', '1_000', 'nan', 'inf' and 'infinity' do not.
The decimal value is rounded to the nearest float, ties to even, however many digits it has.
A value too large to be finite returns the fallback. A value too small to represent is 0.0. '-0' is 0.0.

entries.name: TO_BIG
entries.summary: Widen an int to a bigint

notes: Every int is a bigint, so this never fails and never changes the value.
int and bigint never mix: ADD takes two ints and ADD_BIG takes two bigints. This is how an int crosses over.

entries.name: BIG_TO_INT
entries.summary: Narrow a bigint to an int

notes: A value outside the 64-bit signed range is an overflow error. It never wraps or saturates.

entries.name: ADD_BIG
entries.summary: Add two bigints

notes: bigint is an exact whole number of up to 4000 decimal digits. There is no rounding and no wrapping.
A result with more than 4000 decimal digits is an overflow error. Every bigint address that can grow checks this, so Python and Rust fail at exactly the same place.

entries.name: SUB_BIG
entries.summary: Subtract the second bigint from the first

notes: A result with more than 4000 decimal digits is an overflow error. Every bigint address that can grow checks this, so Python and Rust fail at exactly the same place.
Zero has one sign: 5 - 5 is 0, never -0.

entries.name: MUL_BIG
entries.summary: Multiply two bigints

notes: A result with more than 4000 decimal digits is an overflow error. Every bigint address that can grow checks this, so Python and Rust fail at exactly the same place.

entries.name: DIV_BIG
entries.summary: Divide one bigint by another, truncating toward zero

notes: TRUNCATES TOWARD ZERO, exactly as DIV (400-0000004) does: -7 / 2 is -3, not -4. A Python backend must NOT use //.
The quotient is never larger than the dividend, so this cannot overflow.

entries.name: MOD_BIG
entries.summary: Remainder of dividing one bigint by another

notes: SIGN OF THE DIVIDEND, exactly as MOD (400-0000005) does: -7 mod 2 is -1, not 1. A Python backend must NOT use %.
Consistent with DIV_BIG (400-0000028) so that a == DIV_BIG(a,b)*b + MOD_BIG(a,b).

entries.name: POW_BIG
entries.summary: Raise a bigint to a whole-number power

notes: POW_BIG(x, 0) is 1 for every x, including POW_BIG(0, 0).
A negative exponent is an error, not a fraction.
Overflow is an error exactly when the true result has more than 4000 decimal digits. POW_BIG(10, 3999) fits; POW_BIG(10, 4000) does not.
A backend must not build an intermediate of more than 8000 digits before noticing an overflow: the exponent is an int, and 2 to the power 2^62 would never finish.

entries.name: PARSE_BIG
entries.summary: Read a bigint from text, with a fallback

notes: Never fails; unparseable text returns the fallback.
The same grammar as PARSE_INT (400-0000009): optional leading '-' or '+' then ASCII digits, with surrounding whitespace trimmed first. Underscores, other digit systems, and other bases are rejected.
Leading zeros do not count toward the 4000-digit ceiling. More than 4000 digits after them returns the fallback.

entries.name: GCD
entries.summary: The greatest common divisor of two integers

notes: The result is never negative: GCD(-12, 18) is 6. Signs of the inputs do not matter.
GCD(a, 0) is the absolute value of a, and GCD(0, 0) is 0.

When the true answer is 9223372036854775808 it does not fit, so it is an overflow error. That happens only when one input is the smallest 64-bit integer and the other is 0 or that same number. Python's math.gcd would return the bigger number; Rust's unsigned_abs would hold it but not convert back.

entries.name: LCM
entries.summary: The least common multiple of two integers

notes: The result is never negative: LCM(-4, 6) is 12. Signs of the inputs do not matter.
LCM(a, 0) is 0 for every a, including LCM(0, 0).
Overflow is an error whenever the true answer does not fit in 64 bits. A backend must divide by the GCD before multiplying, so it never builds a product bigger than the answer.

entries.name: PRODUCT
entries.summary: Multiply together a list of integers

notes: An empty list multiplies to 1.

Multiplied left to right, like SUM (400-0000008). Overflow is an error the moment a running product does not fit, even when a later 0 would have brought the answer back: PRODUCT([9223372036854775807, 2, 0]) is an overflow error, not 0.

entries.name: IS_EVEN
entries.summary: Whether an integer is even

notes: Negative numbers follow the same rule: -4 is even and -3 is not. Zero is even.
Never fails, including on the smallest 64-bit integer, which is even.

entries.name: IS_ODD
entries.summary: Whether an integer is odd

notes: Negative numbers follow the same rule: -3 is odd. A backend must not test the remainder against 1, because Rust's -3 % 2 is -1.
Always the opposite of IS_EVEN (400-0000035). Never fails.

entries.name: TO_DEC
entries.summary: Widen an int to a decimal

notes: The result has no places: 12 becomes 12, not 12.0. ROUND_DEC (400-0000047) gives it places.
Never fails and never changes the value.
int and decimal never mix: ADD takes two ints and ADD_DEC takes two decimals. This is how an int crosses over.

entries.name: BIG_TO_DEC
entries.summary: Widen a bigint to a decimal

notes: The result has no places. Never fails: a bigint has at most 4000 digits, and so may a decimal.

entries.name: DEC_TO_INT
entries.summary: Drop a decimal's fractional part to get an int

notes: TRUNCATES TOWARD ZERO, as TO_INT (400-0000020) does: 2.9 is 2 and -2.9 is -2. Use ROUND_DEC with 0 places first for nearest.
A value whose truncation does not fit a 64-bit signed integer is an overflow error. It never wraps or saturates.

entries.name: ADD_DEC
entries.summary: Add two decimals exactly

notes: decimal is an exact base-10 number: a whole-number coefficient and a scale, the count of digits after the point. 0.10 + 0.20 is exactly 0.30.
The result's scale is the larger of the two: 1.5 + 0.25 is 1.75, and 0.10 + 0.20 is 0.30, never 0.3.
A result with more than 4000 digits, or more than 1000 of them after the point, is an overflow error. Every decimal address that can grow checks this.

entries.name: SUB_DEC
entries.summary: Subtract the second decimal from the first, exactly

notes: The result's scale is the larger of the two: 1 - 0.01 is 0.99.
A result with more than 4000 digits, or more than 1000 of them after the point, is an overflow error.
Zero has one sign: 0.5 - 0.5 is 0.0, never -0.0.

entries.name: MUL_DEC
entries.summary: Multiply two decimals exactly

notes: EXACT: nothing is rounded. The scales add, so 1.5 x 0.25 is 0.375 and 19.99 x 3 is 59.97. Use ROUND_DEC (400-0000047) to get back to a number of places.
A result with more than 4000 digits, or more than 1000 of them after the point, is an overflow error.

entries.name: DIV_DEC
entries.summary: Divide two decimals, rounded to a number of places
entries.description: Most quotients have no exact decimal form (1 / 3), so this address takes the number of places to keep and rounds once, halves away from zero, as ROUND does.

notes: The exact quotient a / b, rounded ONCE to exactly `places` digits after the point. HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO: 1 / 8 to 2 places is 0.13, and -1 / 8 is -0.13.
The result always has `places` places, even when the quotient is exact: 1 / 4 to 3 places is 0.250.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error. A zero divisor is a division_by_zero error.
A result with more than 4000 digits is an overflow error.

entries.name: ROUND_DEC
entries.summary: Round a decimal to a number of places, halves away from zero
entries.description: Sets a decimal's places: fewer rounds, more pads with zeros. Rounding is pinned to halves away from zero, the same as ROUND (400-0000021), NOT Python's round() or decimal default, which send halves to even.

notes: The result has exactly `places` digits after the point. HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO: 2.345 to 2 places is 2.35, -2.345 is -2.35, and 2.5 to 0 places is 3.
More places than the value has pads with zeros, exactly: 5 to 2 places is 5.00.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error.
Rounding can add a digit (9.99 to 1 place is 10.0), so a result with more than 4000 digits is an overflow error.
NO NEGATIVE ZERO: -0.004 to 2 places is 0.00.

entries.name: PARSE_DEC
entries.summary: Read a decimal from text, with a fallback

notes: Never fails; unparseable text returns the fallback.

Grammar: optional leading '-' or '+', ASCII digits, then optionally '.' and more ASCII digits, with surrounding whitespace trimmed first. '.5', '5.', exponents, underscores and thousands separators are rejected.
The places are kept as written: '1.50' is 1.50, not 1.5.
Leading zeros do not count toward the 4000-digit ceiling. More than 4000 digits after them, or more than 1000 after the point, returns the fallback.

entries.name: DEC_TO_FLOAT
entries.summary: Convert a decimal to the nearest float

notes: The float nearest the decimal's exact value, ties to even, the way PARSE_FLOAT reads its digits. 0.1 becomes the float that prints as 0.1.
A value too large to be a finite float is an overflow error. A value too small becomes 0.0, never -0.0.

entries.name: FLOAT_TO_DEC
entries.summary: Convert a float to the decimal it prints as

notes: The result is the float's SHORTEST DIGITS, the ones TO_TEXT prints, never its exact binary value: 0.1 becomes 0.1, not 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625.
With those digits d1...dn and exponent E, the result is d1...dn x 10^(E-n+1), with no places when that power is not negative: 2.5 is 2.5, 100.0 is 100, and 1e+16 is 10000000000000000.
Never fails: a float has at most 17 significant digits and E is between -324 and 308, inside both decimal ceilings.

entries.name: NUMBER_EQUALS
entries.summary: True when two numbers of the same type are equal

notes: Both arguments have the same type: an int is never compared with a float. Works for int, bigint, float, decimal and fraction.
Decimals are equal by value, so 0.3 equals 0.30. Fractions are always in lowest terms, so 2/4 equals 1/2.
EXACT. For floats this is equality of the binary value, so 0.1 + 0.2 does not equal 0.3. Use CLOSE_TO (400-0000065) for computed floats.
There is one zero and no NaN, so every float equals itself and nothing else is equal to it.

entries.name: NUMBER_NOT_EQUALS
entries.summary: True when two numbers of the same type are different

notes: Exactly the opposite of NUMBER_EQUALS (400-0000060), with the same exactness for floats.
Works for int, bigint, float, decimal and fraction; decimals compare by value, so 0.3 and 0.30 are equal.

entries.name: LESS_OR_EQUAL
entries.summary: True when the first number is less than or equal to the second

notes: Numeric order, the same order as LESS_THAN (600-0000005). Both arguments have the same type.
True exactly when LESS_THAN(a, b) or NUMBER_EQUALS(a, b) is true.
Works for int, bigint, float, decimal and fraction; decimals compare by value, so 0.3 and 0.30 are equal.

entries.name: GREATER_OR_EQUAL
entries.summary: True when the first number is greater than or equal to the second

notes: Numeric order, the same order as GREATER_THAN (600-0000006). Both arguments have the same type.
True exactly when GREATER_THAN(a, b) or NUMBER_EQUALS(a, b) is true.
Works for int, bigint, float, decimal and fraction; decimals compare by value, so 0.3 and 0.30 are equal.

entries.name: COMPARE
entries.summary: Compare two numbers: -1 if the first is smaller, 0 if equal, 1 if larger

notes: Returns exactly -1, 0, or 1, never another negative or positive number. Never fails.
Numeric order, the same order as LESS_THAN (600-0000005). 0 means NUMBER_EQUALS (400-0000060) is true.
Python has no cmp() and Rust's cmp returns an Ordering, not a number; the contract picks the integers.
Works for int, bigint, float, decimal and fraction; decimals compare by value, so 0.3 and 0.30 are equal.

entries.name: CLOSE_TO
entries.summary: True when two floats are within a tolerance of each other

notes: ABSOLUTE tolerance: true when |a - b| <= tolerance, with a - b rounded to the nearest float. Not Python's math.isclose, which is relative by default.
The tolerance is included, so a tolerance of 0.0 is exact equality.
A negative tolerance is never met: the result is false. Never fails.
When a - b is too large to be finite the two are not close: the result is false, not an overflow error.

entries.name: MAKE_FRACTION
entries.summary: Build an exact fraction from a numerator and a denominator
entries.description: The way into the fraction type. A fraction is an exact ratio of two 64-bit integers that never rounds: 1/3 stays 1/3.

notes: EVERY FRACTION IS KEPT IN LOWEST TERMS WITH A POSITIVE DENOMINATOR. 2/4 becomes 1/2, 3/-6 becomes -1/2, and 0/5 becomes 0/1, so each value has exactly one form.
A zero denominator is a division_by_zero error.
The numerator and denominator of the lowest-terms form must each fit in a 64-bit signed integer, or it is an overflow error: -9223372036854775808 / -1 overflows.
This applies to every fraction address: the working is exact, and only the lowest-terms result has to fit.

entries.name: ADD_FRACTION
entries.summary: Add two fractions exactly

notes: Exact: 1/10 + 2/10 is 3/10. The result is in lowest terms and is an overflow error if that does not fit in 64 bits, as MAKE_FRACTION (400-0000080) says.

entries.name: SUB_FRACTION
entries.summary: Subtract one fraction from another exactly

notes: a - b, exact. The result is in lowest terms and is an overflow error if that does not fit in 64 bits, as MAKE_FRACTION (400-0000080) says.

entries.name: MUL_FRACTION
entries.summary: Multiply two fractions exactly

notes: Exact. The result is in lowest terms and is an overflow error if that does not fit in 64 bits, as MAKE_FRACTION (400-0000080) says.

entries.name: DIV_FRACTION
entries.summary: Divide one fraction by another exactly

notes: a / b, exact: nothing is truncated or rounded. 1/1 divided by 3/1 is 1/3.
Dividing by a zero fraction is a division_by_zero error.
The result is in lowest terms and is an overflow error if that does not fit in 64 bits, as MAKE_FRACTION (400-0000080) says.

entries.name: NEGATE_FRACTION
entries.summary: Flip the sign of a fraction

notes: A fraction whose numerator is -9223372036854775808 has no positive twin in 64 bits, so negating it is an overflow error, as NEGATE (400-0000011) is for int.

entries.name: ABS_FRACTION
entries.summary: The distance of a fraction from zero

notes: A fraction whose numerator is -9223372036854775808 has no positive twin in 64 bits, so its absolute value is an overflow error, as ABS (400-0000010) is for int.

entries.name: NUMERATOR
entries.summary: The top number of a fraction in lowest terms

notes: Of the lowest-terms form, and it carries the sign: the numerator of MAKE_FRACTION(2, -4) is -1.

entries.name: DENOMINATOR
entries.summary: The bottom number of a fraction in lowest terms

notes: Of the lowest-terms form, so it is always at least 1: the denominator of MAKE_FRACTION(2, -4) is 2, and of a whole number it is 1.

entries.name: FRACTION_TO_FLOAT
entries.summary: The float nearest to a fraction

notes: The exact value numerator / denominator, rounded once to the nearest float, ties to even. NOT float(numerator) / float(denominator), which rounds up to three times and can be one step off when either part is past 2^53.
Never fails: every fraction is between -2^63 and 2^63, so the float is finite. Zero is 0.0, never -0.0.

entries.name: FLOOR_FRACTION
entries.summary: The largest whole number not above a fraction

notes: ROUNDS TOWARD NEGATIVE INFINITY, not toward zero: 7/2 gives 3 and -7/2 gives -4. That is Python's //, and NOT Rust's /, which truncates. Never fails: the result is never further from zero than the numerator.

entries.name: ROUND_FRACTION
entries.summary: Round a fraction to the nearest whole number

notes: HALVES GO AWAY FROM ZERO, as in ROUND (400-0000021): 5/2 gives 3 and -5/2 gives -3. Python's round() would give 2 and -2. Never fails: the result is never further from zero than the numerator.

entries.name: PARSE_FRACTION
entries.summary: Read a fraction from text, or a fallback when it is not one

notes: Never fails; unparseable text returns the fallback.

Accepts, after trimming surrounding whitespace: an optional '+' or '-', one or more ASCII digits, and optionally '/' followed by one or more ASCII digits. So '3', '-1/3' and '2/4' parse; '1 / 3', '1/-3', '1.5', '/3' and '1/' do not.
The numerator as written and the denominator as written must each fit in a 64-bit signed integer, and the denominator must not be zero; otherwise the fallback is returned.
The result is in lowest terms: '2/4' reads as 1/2. Whatever TO_TEXT (100-0000005) prints for a fraction reads back as the same fraction.

entries.name: DEC_TO_BIG
entries.summary: Drop a decimal's fractional part to get a bigint

notes: TRUNCATES TOWARD ZERO, as DEC_TO_INT (400-0000042) does: 2.9 is 2 and -2.9 is -2. Use ROUND_DEC with 0 places first for nearest.
Never fails: a decimal has at most 4000 digits, and so may a bigint.

entries.name: BIG_TO_FLOAT
entries.summary: Convert a bigint to the nearest float

notes: The float nearest the bigint's exact value, ties to even, the way PARSE_FLOAT reads its digits. Past 2^53 not every whole number is a float, so 2^53 + 1 becomes 2^53.
A value too large to be a finite float is an overflow error.

entries.name: FLOAT_TO_BIG
entries.summary: Drop a float's fractional part to get a bigint

notes: TRUNCATES TOWARD ZERO, as TO_INT (400-0000020) does: 2.9 is 2 and -2.9 is -2. Use ROUND first for nearest.
The float's EXACT binary value, not its printed digits: 1e23 is 99999999999999991611392, because that is the float 1e23 really is. FLOAT_TO_DEC (400-0000050) is the one that keeps the printed digits.
Never fails: the largest float has 309 digits, well under the bigint ceiling.

entries.name: DEC_TO_FRACTION
entries.summary: Turn a decimal into the exact same fraction

notes: EXACT, in lowest terms: 0.75 is 3/4, 2.50 is 5/2, and -0.10 is -1/10.
When the reduced numerator or denominator does not fit in 64 bits, the result is an overflow error. It never rounds to make it fit.

entries.name: FRACTION_TO_DEC
entries.summary: Turn a fraction into a decimal, rounded to a number of places
entries.description: Most fractions have no exact decimal form (1/3), so this address takes the number of places to keep and rounds once, halves away from zero, as DIV_DEC does.

notes: The exact value numerator / denominator, rounded ONCE to exactly `places` digits after the point. HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO: 1/8 to 2 places is 0.13, and -1/8 is -0.13.
The result always has `places` places, even when the fraction is exact: 1/4 to 3 places is 0.250.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error. Otherwise it never fails.

entries.name: BIG_TO_FRACTION
entries.summary: Turn a bigint into a whole-number fraction

notes: The value over 1: 7 becomes 7, which prints as 7.
A fraction's parts are 64-bit, so a bigint that does not fit a 64-bit signed integer is an overflow error.

entries.name: FORMAT_FLOAT
entries.summary: Print a float with a set number of places, like 3.14
entries.description: Python's format() and Rust's {:.2} both round a float's exact binary value, halves to even, so 2.675 prints as 2.67 (its binary value is just below 2.675). This address rounds the digits TO_TEXT shows instead, halves away from zero, so what you see is what gets rounded: 2.675 prints as 2.68.

notes: ROUNDS THE PRINTED DIGITS, not the binary value: the float's shortest digits, exactly what TO_TEXT (100-0000005) and FLOAT_TO_DEC (400-0000050) give, are rounded to `places`. 2.675 to 2 places is 2.68. A Python backend must NOT use format() or an f-string, and a Rust backend must NOT use {:.N}.
HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO, as ROUND_DEC (400-0000047): 0.125 to 2 places is 0.13 and -0.125 is -0.13. 2.5 to 0 places is 3. More places than the float has pads with zeros: 3.0 to 2 places is 3.00.

Always plain digits with exactly `places` digits after the point and no point when `places` is 0. NEVER an exponent: 1e+20 to 1 place is 100000000000000000000.0. NEVER a negative zero: a value that rounds to zero prints without a minus sign.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error.

entries.name: FORMAT_DEC
entries.summary: Print a decimal with a set number of places, like 19.99
entries.description: The same as ROUND_DEC (400-0000047) followed by TO_TEXT, halves away from zero, NOT Python's round() or decimal default, which send halves to even.

notes: HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO: 2.345 to 2 places is 2.35, -2.345 is -2.35, and 2.5 to 0 places is 3. More places pads with zeros: 5 to 2 places is 5.00.

Always plain digits with exactly `places` digits after the point and no point when `places` is 0. NEVER an exponent: 1e+20 to 1 place is 100000000000000000000.0. NEVER a negative zero: a value that rounds to zero prints without a minus sign. Never an overflow: unlike ROUND_DEC the result is text, so it has no 4000-digit ceiling.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error.

entries.name: FORMAT_FRACTION
entries.summary: Print a fraction as a decimal with a set number of places, like 0.33
entries.description: Prints the fraction's exact value as a decimal, rounded once. 1/3 to 2 places is 0.33, and 2/3 is 0.67. Nothing goes through a float, so 1/3 to 30 places is thirty 3s.

notes: EXACT, ROUNDED ONCE: the result is the fraction's exact value rounded to `places`, never via a float. 1/3 to 4 places is 0.3333 and 2/3 is 0.6667.
HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO, as ROUND_FRACTION (400-0000091): 1/8 to 2 places is 0.13 and -1/8 is -0.13. 5/2 to 0 places is 3.

Always plain digits with exactly `places` digits after the point and no point when `places` is 0. NEVER an exponent: 1e+20 to 1 place is 100000000000000000000.0. NEVER a negative zero: a value that rounds to zero prints without a minus sign.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error.

entries.name: SQRT
entries.summary: Square root of a float
entries.description: Worked out by hand on whole numbers in both runtimes, not with a host sqrt, so the two agree bit for bit by construction.

notes: The exact square root, rounded ONCE to the nearest float, ties to even. This is the correctly rounded root IEEE 754 asks for: SQRT(2.0) is 1.4142135623730951.
A NEGATIVE INPUT IS A negative_root ERROR, never NaN. -0.0 is zero, and its root is 0.0, never -0.0.
Never overflows: the root of the largest float is finite, and the root of the smallest is a normal float.

entries.name: FLOOR
entries.summary: Round a float down to a whole number

notes: TOWARD NEGATIVE INFINITY: 2.7 is 2.0 and -2.3 is -3.0.
The result is a float. Use TO_INT (400-0000020) to get an int. NO NEGATIVE ZERO: -0.0 gives 0.0.

entries.name: CEIL
entries.summary: Round a float up to a whole number

notes: TOWARD POSITIVE INFINITY: 2.3 is 3.0 and -2.7 is -2.0.
The result is a float. NO NEGATIVE ZERO: -0.5 gives 0.0, where both hosts' own ceil would give -0.0.

entries.name: MOD_FLOAT
entries.summary: Remainder of dividing one float by another, sign of the dividend
entries.description: The float companion of MOD (400-0000005). Python's % takes the sign of the divisor, so a Python backend must not use it.

notes: a - b x trunc(a / b), worked out EXACTLY, never rounded: the answer is always a float. This is C's fmod.
SIGN OF THE DIVIDEND: -7.5 mod 2.0 is -1.5, and 7.5 mod -2.0 is 1.5.
A ZERO DIVISOR IS A division_by_zero ERROR, never NaN. NO NEGATIVE ZERO: -4.0 mod 2.0 is 0.0.

entries.name: ISQRT
entries.summary: Square root of an int, rounded down

notes: ROUNDED DOWN: the largest r with r x r <= value. ISQRT(17) is 4.
Worked out on whole numbers, never through a float, so it is exact at every size: ISQRT(9223372036854775807) is 3037000499.
A negative input is a negative_root error.

entries.name: ISQRT_BIG
entries.summary: Square root of a bigint, rounded down

notes: ROUNDED DOWN: the largest r with r x r <= value. Exact at every size; the root has about half the digits, so it never overflows.
A negative input is a negative_root error.

entries.name: SQRT_DEC
entries.summary: Square root of a decimal, rounded to a number of places
entries.description: Most roots have no exact decimal form, so, like DIV_DEC (400-0000046), this address takes the number of places to keep and rounds once.

notes: The exact square root, rounded ONCE to exactly `places` digits after the point, HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO, as ROUND_DEC: the root of 2.25 to 0 places is 2, and of 0.0025 to 1 place is 0.1.
The result always has `places` places, even when the root is exact: the root of 4 to 2 places is 2.00.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error. A negative input is a negative_root error.
A result with more than 4000 digits is an overflow error.

entries.name: FLOOR_DEC
entries.summary: Round a decimal down to a whole number

notes: TOWARD NEGATIVE INFINITY: 2.7 is 2 and -2.3 is -3. The result has no places.
NO NEGATIVE ZERO: -0.5 gives -1, and -0.00 gives 0.
Only a value near the 4000-digit ceiling can overflow.

entries.name: CEIL_DEC
entries.summary: Round a decimal up to a whole number

notes: TOWARD POSITIVE INFINITY: 2.3 is 3 and -2.7 is -2. The result has no places.
NO NEGATIVE ZERO: -0.5 gives 0.
Rounding up can add a digit (9.1 is 10), so a result with more than 4000 digits is an overflow error.

entries.name: MOD_DEC
entries.summary: Remainder of dividing one decimal by another, sign of the dividend

notes: a - b x trunc(a / b), EXACT. The result has the larger of the two scales, as ADD_DEC: 7.50 mod 2 is 1.50.
SIGN OF THE DIVIDEND, as MOD (400-0000005): -7.5 mod 2 is -1.5, and 7.5 mod -2.25 is 0.75.
A ZERO DIVISOR IS A division_by_zero ERROR. The remainder is never larger than either input, so it never overflows.

entries.name: CEIL_FRACTION
entries.summary: The smallest whole number not below a fraction

notes: ROUNDS TOWARD POSITIVE INFINITY: 7/2 gives 4 and -7/2 gives -3. The companion of FLOOR_FRACTION (400-0000090). Never fails: the result is never further from zero than the numerator.

entries.name: MOD_FRACTION
entries.summary: Remainder of dividing one fraction by another, sign of the dividend

notes: a - b x trunc(a / b), EXACT and in lowest terms: 7/2 mod 1/3 is 1/6.
SIGN OF THE DIVIDEND, as MOD (400-0000005): -7/2 mod 1/3 is -1/6, and 7/2 mod -1/3 is 1/6.
A ZERO DIVISOR IS A division_by_zero ERROR. The result's denominator can grow to the product of the two, so one that no longer fits in 64 bits is an overflow error.

entries.name: SMALLEST
entries.summary: The smallest number in a list, of any number type

notes: Works for int, bigint, float, decimal and fraction, in the order COMPARE (400-0000064) uses. MIN (400-0000006) is the two-int version.

TIES GO TO THE FIRST: when several values are equal, the one that comes first in the list is returned. That only shows for decimals, where 0.3 and 0.30 are equal but print differently: SMALLEST([0.30, 0.3]) is 0.30.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no smallest of nothing.

entries.name: LARGEST
entries.summary: The largest number in a list, of any number type

notes: Works for int, bigint, float, decimal and fraction, in the order COMPARE (400-0000064) uses. MAX (400-0000007) is the two-int version.

TIES GO TO THE FIRST: when several values are equal, the one that comes first in the list is returned. That only shows for decimals, where 0.3 and 0.30 are equal but print differently: LARGEST([0.30, 0.3]) is 0.30.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no largest of nothing.

entries.name: SUM_FLOAT
entries.summary: Add up a list of floats, left to right

notes: ADDED LEFT TO RIGHT, EACH STEP ROUNDED as ADD_FLOAT (400-0000015) rounds. NOT a compensated sum: SUM_FLOAT([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]) is 0.6000000000000001. Python 3.12's sum() and math.fsum would say 0.6; neither is used.
An empty list sums to 0.0. A running sum that is not finite is an overflow error.

entries.name: SUM_BIG
entries.summary: Add up a list of bigints

notes: EXACT. An empty list sums to 0.

Only the final total has to fit the 4000-digit ceiling; a running total may pass it on the way, so [10^3999 x 9, 10^3999 x 9, -(10^3999 x 9)] is fine. A total with more than 4000 digits is an overflow error.

entries.name: SUM_DEC
entries.summary: Add up a list of decimals exactly

notes: EXACT: 0.10 + 0.20 + 0.30 is 0.60. The total has the largest scale in the list, as ADD_DEC (400-0000043) keeps the larger of two: [1.5, 0.25] sums to 1.75, and [1, 2.00] to 3.00.
An empty list sums to 0, with no places.
Only the final total has to fit the 4000-digit ceiling; a running total may pass it on the way. A total with more than 4000 digits is an overflow error.

entries.name: SUM_FRACTION
entries.summary: Add up a list of fractions exactly

notes: EXACT and in lowest terms: 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 is 1. An empty list sums to 0.

ADDED LEFT TO RIGHT with ADD_FRACTION (400-0000081). Overflow is an error the moment a running total does not fit in a 64-bit fraction, even when a later value would have brought it back, as for SUM (400-0000008).

entries.name: AVERAGE
entries.summary: The average of a list of integers, as a decimal to a number of places

notes: The exact sum divided by the count, rounded ONCE to exactly `places` digits after the point, HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO, as DIV_DEC (400-0000046): the average of [1, 2] to 0 places is 2, and of [-1, -2] is -2.
The sum is exact and never overflows, however large the ints are.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no average of nothing.

entries.name: AVERAGE_FLOAT
entries.summary: The average of a list of floats

notes: SUM_FLOAT (400-0000182) of the list, then divided by the count, rounded as DIV_FLOAT (400-0000018). So the sum is added left to right with each step rounded, not compensated.
A running sum that is not finite is an overflow error, even when the average would fit.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no average of nothing.

entries.name: AVERAGE_BIG
entries.summary: The average of a list of bigints, as a decimal to a number of places

notes: The exact sum divided by the count, rounded ONCE to exactly `places` digits after the point, HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO, as AVERAGE (400-0000186).
The sum is exact and is not held to the 4000-digit ceiling; only the average is. An average with more than 4000 digits is an overflow error.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no average of nothing.

entries.name: AVERAGE_DEC
entries.summary: The average of a list of decimals, to a number of places

notes: The exact sum divided by the count, rounded ONCE to exactly `places` digits after the point, HALVES AWAY FROM ZERO, as DIV_DEC (400-0000046): the average of [0.01, 0.02] to 2 places is 0.02.
The result always has `places` places, whatever scales the values have.
The sum is exact and is not held to the 4000-digit ceiling; only the average is. An average with more than 4000 digits is an overflow error.
`places` must be between 0 and 1000, or it is an invalid_places error.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no average of nothing.

entries.name: AVERAGE_FRACTION
entries.summary: The exact average of a list of fractions

notes: EXACT and in lowest terms: SUM_FRACTION (400-0000185) of the list divided by the count. The average of 1/2 and 1/3 is 5/12.
The sum can overflow as SUM_FRACTION says, and so can the division, when the count times the denominator does not reduce back into 64 bits.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no average of nothing.

entries.name: MEDIAN
entries.summary: The middle value of a list of integers, as an exact decimal

notes: The list is sorted, smallest first. An ODD count gives the middle value, with no places. An EVEN count gives the exact midpoint of the two middle values: [1, 3] gives 2, and [1, 2] gives 1.5, with one place only when it is needed.
Never rounded, so the answer is always exact, and it never overflows.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no median of nothing.

entries.name: MEDIAN_FLOAT
entries.summary: The middle value of a list of floats

notes: The list is sorted, smallest first. An ODD count gives the middle value. An EVEN count gives the exact midpoint of the two middle values, ROUNDED ONCE to the nearest float, ties to even.
The midpoint NEVER OVERFLOWS: the median of two values near the largest float is still a finite float, even though their sum is not.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no median of nothing.

entries.name: MEDIAN_BIG
entries.summary: The middle value of a list of bigints, as an exact decimal

notes: The same rule as MEDIAN (400-0000191): an ODD count gives the middle value, with no places; an EVEN count gives the exact midpoint of the two middle values, with one place only when it is needed.
A midpoint of two values near the 4000-digit ceiling can need 4001 digits once it has a place, which is an overflow error.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no median of nothing.

entries.name: MEDIAN_DEC
entries.summary: The middle value of a list of decimals, exactly

notes: The list is sorted by value, smallest first, and equal values keep their list order (a stable sort, as SORT). An ODD count gives the middle value exactly as it is, places and all.
An EVEN count gives the exact midpoint of the two middle values, at the larger of their two scales, plus one place only when it is needed: [1.0, 3.0] gives 2.0, and [0.01, 0.02] gives 0.015.
Never rounded. A midpoint with more than 1000 places or 4000 digits is an overflow error.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no median of nothing.

entries.name: MEDIAN_FRACTION
entries.summary: The middle value of a list of fractions, exactly

notes: The list is sorted, smallest first. An ODD count gives the middle value. An EVEN count gives the exact midpoint of the two middle values, in lowest terms: 1/3 and 1/2 give 5/12.
A midpoint whose lowest terms do not fit in a 64-bit fraction is an overflow error.
AN EMPTY LIST IS AN empty_list ERROR: there is no median of nothing.
